neuassyrisches-reich#text: From 911 BC the kings of Assyria on the upper Tigris extended their rule through annual campaigns; Ashurnasirpal II built Nimrud into a magnificent residence, and Tiglath-Pileser III created a standing army and a system of provinces. The Assyrians deployed siege engines, cavalry and iron weapons, deported subjugated peoples and deliberately spread terror through reliefs and inscriptions. At its height in the 7th century BC the empire reached from Egypt to Iran; at Nineveh, Ashurbanipal assembled the first great library, with more than 30,000 clay tablets, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. In 612 BC Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh, and the empire collapsed.
chavin-kultur-in-peru#summary: In the Andes, Chavín de Huántar becomes a pilgrimage center whose art and religion shape large parts of Peru.
chavin-kultur-in-peru#text: Chavín de Huántar lies at an altitude of more than 3,000 meters in the Peruvian Andes, at the confluence of two rivers. From about 900 BC the people there built a temple of stone with underground passages, water channels and the Lanzón, a stone pillar four and a half meters high bearing the image of a deity with the fangs of a predator. Pilgrims from across the Andean region brought shells from the coast, obsidian and textiles; in the temple, priests played shell trumpets and used hallucinogenic cacti in rituals. The Chavín style, with jaguars, snakes and eagles, spread through pottery, gold and textiles and is regarded as the first shared culture of the Andes, out of which the Moche, Nazca and Inca later emerged.
paracas-kultur#title: Paracas: mummy bundles and magnificent textiles
paracas-kultur#summary: On the south coast of Peru the Paracas culture wraps its dead in artfully woven mantles.
paracas-kultur#text: On the desert peninsula of Paracas, the Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello discovered large cemeteries in the 1920s. The dead had been wrapped in a crouching position in many layers of cloth, including embroidered mantles showing gods, animals and warriors in brilliant colors. In the dry climate these fabrics survived exceptionally well. Skulls show artificial shaping and healed openings in the skull that point to medical operations. The Paracas culture later gave rise to the Nazca culture on the south coast.
erste-olympische-spiele#summary: The first recorded contests in honor of Zeus are held at Olympia.
erste-olympische-spiele#text: According to tradition the first games were held in 776 BC at Olympia in the Peloponnese; the only event was a race the length of the stadium. Every four years athletes came together from across the Greek world, and a sacred truce was in force for the duration of the games. The Greeks reckoned time in Olympiads, and the games were not banned until AD 393, by the Christian emperor Theodosius.
gruendung-roms#summary: According to legend, Romulus founds the city of Rome on the Tiber.
gruendung-roms#text: According to Roman tradition, Romulus, who is said to have been suckled by a she-wolf, founded the city of Rome in the year 753 BC. Archaeologically, settlement of the hills by the Tiber can be traced from the 10th century BC. The Romans counted their years from this date of foundation, ab urbe condita.
griechische-kolonisation#summary: Greek cities found hundreds of colonies from Spain to the Black Sea and spread the language, writing and way of life of the Greeks.
griechische-kolonisation#text: Shortage of land, hunger, trade and internal conflict led many poleis to send out citizens and found new cities: Cyme and Syracuse in Italy and Sicily, Massalia, today's Marseille, Cyrene in North Africa, Byzantion on the Bosporus and numerous cities on the Black Sea. The colonies were politically independent but remained tied to their mother city through cults, language and trade. Southern Italy and Sicily thus became Magna Graecia, Greater Greece, where thinkers such as Pythagoras and Archimedes were active. Colonization brought the Greeks into contact with Etruscans, Celts, Scythians and Egyptians and passed the alphabet and the coin on to their neighbors.
homer-und-die-epen#title: Homer and the Epics Iliad and Odyssey
homer-und-die-epen#summary: The epics about the Trojan War and the wanderings of Odysseus are set down in writing.
homer-und-die-epen#text: The Iliad and the Odyssey, attributed to the poet Homer, gathered orally transmitted legends about the Trojan War into artful hexameters. They were the foundation of Greek education, shaped the image of the gods and heroes, and were revered as a model from Alexander the Great to the Romans. At the same time the Greeks adopted the Phoenician alphabet and added vowels to it.
orakel-von-delphi#title: Delphi and the Oracle of Apollo
orakel-von-delphi#summary: The sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi becomes the most important oracle site of the Greek world, consulted by cities and kings before every major decision.
orakel-von-delphi#text: On the slope of Mount Parnassus the priestess Pythia, seated on a tripod, proclaimed the answers of the god Apollo, which the priests cast into often ambiguous verse. From the 8th century BC at the latest, poleis sought the advice of Delphi before founding colonies, going to war and reforming their laws, and foreigners too, such as the Lydian king Croesus, sent envoys and votive offerings. The Greek cities erected treasuries there, and from 582 BC the Pythian Games were held, with contests in music and athletics. The maxims Know thyself and Nothing in excess at the temple entrance summed up Greek practical wisdom; Delphi was regarded as the navel of the world and was not closed until AD 391.
reformen-solons#title: The Reforms of Solon in Athens
reformen-solons#summary: Solon abolishes debt bondage and grants all citizens of Athens political rights according to their wealth.
reformen-solons#text: Around 594 BC the poet and statesman Solon was charged with resolving the crisis in Athens, in which indebted farmers had fallen into slavery. He cancelled all debts, forbade the enslavement of citizens for debt, and bought back those who had been carried off. He divided the citizens according to their harvest yield into four classes, which received graduated rights to hold office; even the poorest class was allowed to take part in the assembly and the courts. Solon refused to become a tyrant and left Athens for ten years so that his laws would be put to the test. He is regarded as one of the Seven Sages and as a forerunner of democracy.
kyros-gruendet-das-perserreich#title: Cyrus II Founds the Persian Empire
kyros-gruendet-das-perserreich#summary: Cyrus defeats the Medes and founds the Achaemenid Empire, the largest empire of its time.
kyros-gruendet-das-perserreich#text: Around 550 BC Cyrus II overthrew the Median king Astyages and united Persians and Medes under his rule. In the years that followed he conquered Lydia with its fabulously wealthy king Croesus, and in 539 BC Babylon, where he permitted the deported Jews to return to Jerusalem. His successors extended the empire as far as Egypt and the Indus and administered it through satrapies, royal roads and an imperial postal service.
tyrannis-der-peisistratiden#title: The Tyranny of the Peisistratids in Athens
tyrannis-der-peisistratiden#summary: Peisistratus and his sons rule Athens as tyrants and promote farmers, festivals and the arts, until Hippias is driven out.
tyrannis-der-peisistratiden#text: After two failed attempts, Peisistratus seized lasting power in Athens around 546 BC with the help of mercenaries. He left Solon's laws in force, granted credit to smallholders, had aqueducts and temples built, and staged the Dionysia with its drama competitions and the Panathenaia as great festivals; under him the epics of Homer were set down in writing. After his death in 527 BC his sons Hippias and Hipparchus followed; after the murder of Hipparchus in 514 BC, Hippias ruled harshly until Spartans and Athenian nobles drove him out in 510 BC. The tyrannicides Harmodius and Aristogeiton became heroes of the young democracy.
beginn-der-roemischen-republik#title: The Beginning of the Roman Republic
beginn-der-roemischen-republik#summary: The Romans drive out their last king and establish a republic.
beginn-der-roemischen-republik#text: After the expulsion of King Tarquinius Superbus, two consuls elected annually took over the government. The Senate, the popular assemblies and offices such as praetor, censor and tribune of the plebs formed a system of mutual checks. The Conflict of the Orders between patricians and plebeians led over two centuries to greater rights for the common people, for example through the Law of the Twelve Tables around 450 BC.
reformen-des-kleisthenes#title: The Reforms of Cleisthenes and the Beginning of Democracy
reformen-des-kleisthenes#summary: Cleisthenes reorganizes the citizenry of Athens and lays the foundation of Athenian democracy.
reformen-des-kleisthenes#text: After the fall of the tyranny of the Peisistratids, Cleisthenes divided the citizens of Athens into ten new tribes that mixed city, coast and inland and broke the power of the old aristocratic families. A Council of 500, filled by lot, prepared the decisions of the assembly; ostracism was meant to prevent any individual from grasping too much power. Under Pericles the democracy was later expanded, but it remained restricted to male citizens.
buddha-lehrt-in-nordindien#title: The Buddha Teaches in Northern India
buddha-lehrt-in-nordindien#summary: Siddhartha Gautama proclaims his teaching on the end of suffering in the Ganges valley.
buddha-lehrt-in-nordindien#text: After his enlightenment beneath a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, Siddhartha Gautama gave his first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath on the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. For about four decades he traveled through northern India as a wandering teacher and founded a community of monks and nuns. His teaching opposed the caste system and the sacrificial priesthood and later became one of the great world religions.
daoismus-und-laozi#summary: In China, Daoism emerges as a teaching of harmony with the Dao, the way of nature.
daoismus-und-laozi#text: The Daodejing, attributed to the legendary sage Laozi, teaches in 81 short chapters that people should not act against the order of nature but adapt to it. Instead of rules and ceremonies as with Confucius, it recommends restraint, simplicity and non-action, wuwei, for the ruler as well. Daoism later became a popular religion with temples, priests and a search for immortality, and it influenced Chinese medicine, painting and martial arts.
gruendung-von-monte-alban#summary: On a leveled mountain above the Valley of Oaxaca, the capital of the Zapotecs is built.
gruendung-von-monte-alban#text: Around 500 BC the Zapotecs leveled the top of a mountain in the Valley of Oaxaca and built their new capital there. Around a large plaza they erected temples, palaces, a ball court and an observatory. The stone reliefs of the so-called Dancers, which probably depict slain or captured enemies, are famous, as are early inscriptions that are among the oldest written records in Mesoamerica. Monte Albán remained a center of power for over a thousand years and only lost its importance between AD 700 and 900.
konfuzius-und-seine-lehre#summary: The scholar Confucius sets out an ethics of humaneness, duty and education.
konfuzius-und-seine-lehre#text: In a time of constant war between the Chinese princely states, Confucius taught that order arises through moral example, respect for parents and rulers, and education. His students collected his sayings in the Analects, the Lunyu. Under the Han dynasty, Confucianism became the state doctrine and remained the basis of Chinese civil service training for more than two thousand years.
schlacht-von-marathon#summary: The Athenians defeat a Persian landing force and repel the first attack by the Great King Darius.
schlacht-von-marathon#text: The Persian Great King Darius I sent a fleet to Greece to punish Athens for supporting a revolt in Asia Minor. At Marathon the Athenian hoplites under Miltiades charged the numerically superior Persians at a run and put them to flight. The victory strengthened Athenian self-confidence; the legend of the messenger who ran the news to Athens gave the marathon race its name.
schlacht-an-den-thermopylen#summary: King Leonidas and 300 Spartans hold the pass against the Persian army and fall to the last man.
schlacht-an-den-thermopylen#text: When Xerxes marched into Greece in 480 BC with an enormous army, a Greek force of a few thousand men under the Spartan king Leonidas opposed him at the narrow pass of Thermopylae. For two days the Persian attacks broke against the phalanx of the hoplites. When a traitor showed the Persians a mountain path, Leonidas sent most of the allies away and stayed behind with 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans, all of whom fell. Militarily a defeat, the battle became a symbol of sacrifice for freedom; the epitaph telling the stranger to report to Sparta that here they lie, obedient to her laws, is famous to this day.
schlacht-von-salamis#summary: The Greek fleet under Themistocles destroys the Persian fleet of Xerxes in the strait of Salamis.
schlacht-von-salamis#text: Ten years after Marathon, Xerxes invaded Greece with an enormous army, overcame the Spartans under Leonidas at Thermopylae and destroyed Athens. Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow bay of Salamis, where the agile Greek triremes defeated the superior force. The following year the Greeks also beat the Persian land army at Plataea; Athens rose to become the leading naval power and founded the Delian League.
zeit-der-streitenden-reiche#title: The Warring States Period and Sunzi's Art of War
zeit-der-streitenden-reiche#summary: Seven Chinese states wage war for two and a half centuries while the philosophers of the Hundred Schools argue over the right order.
zeit-der-streitenden-reiche#text: After the collapse of Zhou rule, the states of Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei fought for supremacy with mass armies of infantry, crossbows and iron weapons. In this crisis, thinkers such as Mencius, Mozi, Zhuangzi and the Legalists sought paths to peace and order; they are known as the Hundred Schools of Thought. The strategist Sunzi set out in The Art of War the principles by which a wise commander wins through deception, planning and knowledge of the enemy, ideally without a battle at all. The era ended in 221 BC with the victory of the state of Qin.
aischylos-und-die-tragoedie#title: Aeschylus and the Flowering of Tragedy
aischylos-und-die-tragoedie#summary: With The Persians by Aeschylus, the oldest surviving tragedy is performed; Athenian theater reaches its height.
aischylos-und-die-tragoedie#text: At the Dionysia, the spring festival of the god Dionysus, three poets competed in Athens each year with three tragedies and a satyr play apiece; performances in the Theater of Dionysus on the slope of the Acropolis drew as many as 15,000 spectators. In 472 BC Aeschylus won with The Persians, which shows the Battle of Salamis from the perspective of the defeated and is the oldest surviving drama in world literature. Aeschylus introduced the second actor and thereby made dialogue possible; Sophocles added the third and wrote Antigone and Oedipus the King, while Euripides portrayed human passion and suffering in Medea and The Trojan Women. Theater was part of political life: the state paid citizens' admission, and the plays worked through questions of law, power and guilt.
zwoelftafelgesetz#summary: Rome receives its first written legal code in the Twelve Tables, set up publicly in the Forum.
zwoelftafelgesetz#text: Until the middle of the 5th century BC, only patrician priests and officials knew the law, which left the plebeians exposed to arbitrary treatment. Under their pressure, a commission of ten men, the decemvirs, wrote down the existing law around 450 BC on twelve bronze tables that were set up in the Forum. The provisions governed court procedure, debt, property, family, inheritance and punishment, and some were harsh, for example toward debtors. For the Romans the Twelve Tables remained the origin of their law; schoolchildren still learned them by heart in Cicero's day, and the principle that law must be public and the same for all carried through into modern law.
bau-des-parthenon#title: The Height of Athens: Building the Parthenon
bau-des-parthenon#summary: Under Pericles the Parthenon rises on the Acropolis, the masterpiece of Greek architecture.
bau-des-parthenon#text: After the Persians laid waste to the Acropolis in 480 BC, Pericles pushed through the rebuilding of the temples with the contributions of the Delian League. The architects Ictinus and Callicrates built the Parthenon from 447 to 432 BC out of Pentelic marble, with 46 Doric columns, a 160-meter frieze showing the Panathenaic procession, and inside a twelve-meter statue of Athena in gold and ivory by Phidias. Subtle curves and inclinations of the columns compensate for optical illusions and make the building appear perfect. The temple later became a church and a mosque and was badly damaged by an explosion in 1687; Lord Elgin took a large part of the sculptures to London around 1800, where they remain in the British Museum, still disputed.
peloponnesischer-krieg#summary: Athens and Sparta struggle for almost three decades over supremacy in Greece; Athens loses.
peloponnesischer-krieg#text: The rivalry between the naval power Athens and the land power Sparta led to war in 431 BC, described by the historian Thucydides. A plague carried off Pericles and a large part of the Athenians in 429 BC, and the expedition to Sicily from 415 to 413 BC ended in catastrophe. With Persian money Sparta built a fleet and forced Athens to capitulate in 404 BC; the Greek city-states emerged from the war exhausted.
hippokrates-und-die-medizin#title: Hippocrates and the Beginnings of Scientific Medicine
hippokrates-und-die-medizin#summary: On the island of Kos, Hippocrates founds a medicine that traces illness to natural causes.
hippokrates-und-die-medizin#text: Hippocrates of Kos and his students taught around 420 BC that diseases are not sent by the gods but have natural causes such as climate, diet and way of life. Physicians should observe the sick closely, record the course of the illness and above all do no harm. The roughly 60 writings of the Hippocratic Corpus deal with epidemics, fractures, diet and the doctrine of the four humors, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, which shaped medicine into the modern era. The Hippocratic Oath, which binds physicians to confidentiality and to the good of the patient, remains the foundation of medical ethics today.
prozess-und-tod-des-sokrates#title: The Trial and Death of Socrates
prozess-und-tod-des-sokrates#summary: An Athenian jury court condemns the philosopher Socrates to death by the cup of hemlock.
prozess-und-tod-des-sokrates#text: Socrates was charged with not recognizing the gods of the city and with corrupting the youth. Before 500 jurors he defended himself without pleading for mercy and was convicted by a narrow majority. He refused to flee, because he respected the laws of his city, and drank the cup of poison surrounded by his students. Plato made the trial a foundational text of philosophy in his Apology.
alexanders-feldzug-nach-asien#summary: Alexander the Great conquers the Persian Empire in eleven years and pushes as far as India.
alexanders-feldzug-nach-asien#text: With about 40,000 men, Alexander crossed the Hellespont in 334 BC, defeated the Persians at the Granicus, at Issus and in 331 BC at Gaugamela, and had himself recognized as pharaoh in Egypt. He marched through Persia and Bactria, crossed the Indus and reached the Hyphasis in the Punjab, where his exhausted soldiers forced him to turn back. Alexander founded numerous cities named Alexandria and died in Babylon in 323 BC; his generals, the Diadochi, divided the empire among themselves.
gruendung-alexandrias#title: The Conquest of Egypt and the Founding of Alexandria
gruendung-alexandrias#summary: Alexander is recognized as pharaoh in Egypt and founds Alexandria in the Nile Delta, the future capital of the Hellenistic world.
gruendung-alexandrias#text: After the victory at Issus and the capture of Tyre, Alexander marched into Egypt in 332 BC, where the population received him as a liberator from the Persians and the priests recognized him as pharaoh. At the oasis of Siwa the oracle of Ammon greeted him as the son of the god. In early 331 BC he marked out on the Mediterranean coast west of the Nile Delta the plan of a new city with streets at right angles and two harbors. Under the Ptolemies, Alexandria became the largest city of the Mediterranean world, with its library, its Museion and the lighthouse of Pharos, and it remained a center of trade, scholarship and Greek culture in Egypt into Roman times.
diadochenkriege#summary: Alexander's generals fight over his legacy for four decades until three great kingdoms emerge.
diadochenkriege#text: Alexander left no capable heir when he died in 323 BC; his generals, the Diadochi, divided the satrapies among themselves and fought one another in shifting alliances. Alexander's mother, his wife Roxana and his son were murdered. Antigonus tried to hold the empire together but fell in 301 BC at the Battle of Ipsus; the wars ended with the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BC. Three great realms remained: that of the Ptolemies in Egypt, of the Seleucids in Syria, Mesopotamia and Iran, and of the Antigonids in Macedon, along with smaller states such as Pergamon. These Hellenistic kingdoms shaped the East until the Roman conquest.
el-mirador-maya-vorklassik#title: El Mirador: a great city of the early Maya
el-mirador-maya-vorklassik#summary: Centuries before the Classic period, the Maya build enormous pyramids in northern Guatemala.
el-mirador-maya-vorklassik#text: In the rainforest of the northern Petén lay El Mirador, which flourished in the last centuries BC. By volume, the temple complex of La Danta is among the largest structures of the premodern world. Raised causeways, the sacbeob, linked El Mirador with neighboring cities. Airborne laser scans have shown that the surrounding area was densely settled and crisscrossed with fields, canals and settlements. Around AD 150 the city lost its importance, and power shifted to places such as Tikal and Calakmul.
bibliothek-von-alexandria#title: The Founding of the Library of Alexandria
bibliothek-von-alexandria#summary: The Ptolemies create in Alexandria the largest library and the most important research center of antiquity.
bibliothek-von-alexandria#text: Ptolemy I and his son Ptolemy II had a Museion built in Alexandria with an attached library intended to collect hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Scholars such as Euclid, Eratosthenes, who calculated the circumference of the Earth, and Archimedes worked there or were connected with it. Alexandria became the center of Hellenistic scholarship; the library was lost over the following centuries through fires and neglect.
punische-kriege#summary: In three wars Rome wears Carthage down and becomes the leading power in the western Mediterranean.
punische-kriege#text: In the First Punic War, Rome gained Sicily and built a large fleet for the first time. In the Second, Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and defeated the Romans at Cannae in 216 BC, but lost to Scipio at Zama in 202 BC. The Third Punic War ended in 146 BC with the complete destruction of Carthage.
ashoka-verbreitet-den-buddhismus#title: Ashoka and the Spread of Buddhism
ashoka-verbreitet-den-buddhismus#summary: After a bloody war, the Maurya king Ashoka turns to Buddhism and proclaims a policy of nonviolence.
ashoka-verbreitet-den-buddhismus#text: Ashoka ruled the Maurya Empire, which covered almost the entire Indian subcontinent. By his own account, the suffering of the war against Kalinga around 261 BC moved him to govern thereafter by the principles of Buddhism. On rocks and pillars he had edicts carved about tolerance, welfare and the renunciation of violence, and he sent Buddhist missionaries as far as Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic kingdoms. The lion capital of his pillar at Sarnath is today the state emblem of India.
frueheste-maya-schrift-san-bartolo#title: Earliest Maya writing at San Bartolo
frueheste-maya-schrift-san-bartolo#summa: Murals and glyphs from San Bartolo in Guatemala show that the Maya were already writing in the 3rd century BC.
frueheste-maya-schrift-san-bartolo#text: At the ruined site of San Bartolo in northern Guatemala, archaeologists found colorful murals from 2001 onward that show the maize god and the installation of a king. Beneath a later building they also discovered an inscription dated to about 300 to 200 BC. This meant that Maya writing was much older than long assumed. It consisted of word signs and syllable signs and could render any statement of the language. It was only deciphered in the 20th century, above all thanks to Yuri Knorozov and Tatiana Proskouriakoff.
qin-shihuangdi-einigt-china#title: Qin Shi Huang Unifies China and Begins the Great Wall
qin-shihuangdi-einigt-china#summary: The king of Qin defeats the last rival states and calls himself First Emperor.
qin-shihuangdi-einigt-china#text: After defeating the six remaining Warring States, the king of Qin took the title Shi Huangdi, First August Emperor. He standardized writing, coinage, measures, weights and even the axle width of carts, divided the land into administrative districts, and had existing frontier ramparts joined into a first Great Wall against the mounted nomads in the north. His rule was harsh and rested on the strict doctrine of Legalism; a few years after his death the dynasty fell, but the unified empire endured.
archimedes-und-die-belagerung-von-syraku: Archimedes and the Siege of Syracuse
The war machines of Archimedes hold off the Romans for two years; when the city falls, the scholar is killed.

Syracuse, the most powerful Greek city in Sicily, had sided with Carthage in the Second Punic War. When the Roman commander Marcellus besieged the city in 213 BC, catapults, cranes that lifted ships out of the water and other machines designed by Archimedes are said to have repelled the attackers again and again. In 212 BC the Romans broke into the city during a festival. A soldier killed Archimedes, who was reportedly bent over a geometric drawing, against the orders of Marcellus to spare him. Syracuse was plundered and became part of the Roman province of Sicily; the conquest shows how the Greek world came step by step under Roman rule.
terrakotta-armee#title: The Terracotta Army of the First Emperor
terrakotta-armee#summary: Qin Shi Huang is buried in an enormous tomb complex guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers.
terrakotta-armee#text: Already as a young king, Qin Shi Huang had begun building his tomb at the foot of Mount Li near Xi'an, on which, according to Sima Qian, as many as 700,000 workers were employed at times. After his death in 210 BC he was laid to rest in an underground palace complex surrounded by pits holding about 8,000 warriors, horses and chariots of fired clay. Each figure has its own face, carried real weapons and was originally painted in color. Farmers discovered the army in 1974 while digging a well; the burial mound itself has still not been opened.
scharrbilder-von-nazca#summary: In the desert of southern Peru, the Nazca culture lays out huge lines and animal figures.
scharrbilder-von-nazca#text: On the plateaus near Nazca, people removed the dark, oxidized stones from the surface so that the lighter ground beneath became visible. In this way they created straight lines kilometers long, triangles and figures such as a hummingbird, a monkey and a spider, which are best recognized from the air. The German researcher Maria Reiche devoted her life to surveying and protecting them. The lines probably served rituals, processions and prayers for water. The Nazca also built underground water channels and created richly colored pottery.
rom-erobert-griechenland#summary: With the destruction of Corinth, Greece becomes part of the Roman Empire.
rom-erobert-griechenland#text: After victories over Macedon at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC and Pydna in 168 BC, Rome crushed the revolt of the Achaean League in 146 BC and destroyed Corinth. Greece was first placed under the province of Macedonia and later became the province of Achaea. The Romans nevertheless took over Greek art, literature and philosophy; the poet Horace wrote that captive Greece had captured her rough conqueror.
reformen-der-gracchen#title: The Attempted Reforms of the Gracchi
reformen-der-gracchen#summary: The tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus fail with their land reforms and are killed.
reformen-der-gracchen#text: In 133 BC Tiberius Gracchus wanted to distribute public land to impoverished farmers in order to save the basis of the citizen army. The Senate resisted, Tiberius was beaten to death, and his brother Gaius was driven to his death ten years later. This violence in domestic politics is considered the beginning of the crisis of the Republic.
han-dynastie-und-seidenstrasse#title: The Han Dynasty and the Silk Road
han-dynastie-und-seidenstrasse#summary: Under Emperor Wu, China opens trade routes to Central Asia that link the East with the Mediterranean world.
